app.name: Financert
app.tagline: where the top 1% actually keep their money
app.installHint: Add Financert to your home screen

compare.emptyBody: Add what you hold on the Your portfolio tab and this page will show how your mix compares with {tier}.
compare.allocationSub: Each asset class as a share of the portfolio being compared.
compare.differSub: Percentage points above or below {tier}. Differences under 1.5pp are treated as in line — the underlying survey data is not precise enough to read more finely.
compare.pendingBody: The Federal Reserve releases {classes} later than the rest of the balance sheet, so it appears as “not yet published” below rather than as a number. Every other share is still correct.
compare.differDollars: The dollar column is that gap against your {total}: what it would take to close it.
compare.tryExampleNote: — roughly the median American shape: most of it in the house, a retirement account, a small brokerage balance, against a mortgage. Clearing it is the same button as clearing your own.
compare.slopeSub: Every class as a share, yours on the left and {tier} on the right. Crossing lines are classes the two of you rank differently; classes under 2% are drawn but not labelled.

portfolio.title: Your portfolio
portfolio.intro: Enter what you hold in each category, in dollars. Leave anything you do not hold blank. Values stay in this browser.
portfolio.introLive: Enter what you hold in each category, in dollars. Leave anything you do not hold blank. Values stay in this browser and are saved to the API when you press Save.
portfolio.categoriesHint: Categories match the Federal Reserve's own balance-sheet definitions, so the comparison is like-for-like.
portfolio.savedLocal: Saved in this browser only — the API is unreachable.
portfolio.needsToken: Could not save: this server requires an API token. Add it below.
portfolio.tokenHelp: Only needed when the server sets FINANCERT_API_TOKEN. Stored in this browser and sent as a bearer header. Leave blank for a local server with no token configured.
portfolio.owedSub: Optional. Comparing an allocation needs none of this — it is what lets the app state your net worth, which is the figure the Fed's tiers are defined by.
portfolio.netWorthNote: What you hold less what you owe — the same definition the tiers use.

benchmarks.nestedNote: net worth — counted inside the {tier}, not alongside it
benchmarks.holdTitle: How each tier holds its assets
benchmarks.holdSub: Share of {scope} assets, {quarter}. Each column sums to 100%. The top 0.1% is a subset of the top 1%, not a fifth group.
benchmarks.trendSub: Share of each tier's total assets, since 1989. {first} vs {last} shown; the middle tiers sit between them.
benchmarks.shapeTitle: The shape of each balance sheet
benchmarks.shapeSub: Three ways to describe a tier in one number each, from the same Federal Reserve data as the table above.
benchmarks.leverageNote: Leverage is debt against the whole balance sheet, so it does not change with the investable-only switch. The other two follow whatever the table above is showing.
benchmarks.perHouseholdNote: Each tier's holdings divided by the number of households in it — an average, not a typical household. The spread inside a tier is widest at the top: the top 0.1% is inside the top 1% and holds several times its average.
benchmarks.owesSub: Share of each tier's borrowing, not of its assets. Mortgages dominate the middle; the bottom 50% carries far more of its debt as consumer credit, and the top 1% far more as margin and policy loans.
benchmarks.unallocatedNote: “Unallocated” is the gap between the Fed's published asset total and the categories above it. With the full column set it is rounding — under 0.0002% in every quarter since 1989 — and /api/benchmarks/reconciliation publishes it per quarter so that is checkable rather than asserted.
benchmarks.trendEmpty: The source publishes no history for {asset} on this axis.
benchmarks.scatterSub: The two measures above, plotted against each other. The tiers do not sit on a line: the top of the distribution is both the most concentrated and among the most liquid, because the class it concentrates in is itself liquid.
benchmarks.multiplesTitle: The same mix, group by group
benchmarks.multiplesSub: Each column is one group’s assets, in the same band order. The trade that runs down the distribution is one glance: businesses and equities at the top, a house at the bottom.
benchmarks.compositionSub: Every class as a share, since 1989. The top 1% went from a fifth in equities and a fifth in private business to half in equities — a trade no single line shows. The seven largest classes get their own band; the rest are collected.
benchmarks.compositionNeedsApi: This one needs the API: the embedded snapshot carries annual samples of three classes, which is a trend rather than a composition.

chart.allocationAria: Allocation of {you} compared with {tier}, by asset class
chart.gapAria: Difference in allocation versus {tier}, in percentage points, by asset class
chart.trendAria: {asset} as a share of total assets over time
chart.allInLine: Every asset class is in line with {tier}.
chart.noHistory: No history to show for this series.
chart.pngFailed: This browser would not render the image.
chart.scatterAria: Share held in liquid classes against share in the single largest class, one point per group
chart.scatterNote: Concentration is the share in whichever class is largest for that group — not the same class for each. {you} appears once holdings are entered.
chart.slopeAria: Each asset class as a share, {you} on the left and {tier} on the right
chart.compositionAria: Every asset class as a share of {tier}, quarter by quarter
chart.multiplesAria: Every group’s mix of asset classes, side by side

disclaimer.whatBody: Financert compares a portfolio against how American households actually hold their assets, grouped by net worth and five other cuts of the same households, measured by the Federal Reserve's
disclaimer.newestComplete: ; the newest fully published quarter is {quarter}
disclaimer.notBody: It is descriptive, not advice. Matching the top 1%'s allocation would not reproduce their returns: much of their wealth sits in private businesses they own and run, and the data says nothing about risk, taxes, time horizon, or whether any allocation suits you. Where groups differ, what differs is what they hold; this data records that and does not explain why.

assetBlurbs.corporate_equities: Directly held corporate equities plus mutual fund shares.
assetBlurbs.private_business: Equity in noncorporate business — partnerships and sole proprietorships.
assetBlurbs.pension: Defined benefit and defined contribution pension entitlements.
assetBlurbs.real_estate: Owner-occupied real estate including vacant land and mobile homes.
assetBlurbs.deposits: Checkable deposits and currency, time and savings deposits.
assetBlurbs.debt_securities: Treasury, municipal, corporate and foreign bonds held directly.
assetBlurbs.consumer_durables: Vehicles, appliances, furnishings — counted as assets by the Fed.
assetBlurbs.annuities: Annuities sold by life insurers directly to households.
assetBlurbs.life_insurance: Cash value of life insurance reserves.
assetBlurbs.loans_assets: Mortgages and other loans held as assets.
assetBlurbs.unallocated: Assets the Fed's totals include but do not break out separately.

dimensionNotes.networth: Households grouped by where their net worth falls in the national distribution.
dimensionNotes.generation: Households grouped by the birth cohort of the reference person, using the Federal Reserve's own cohorts.
dimensionNotes.education: Households grouped by the highest level of education the reference person completed.
dimensionNotes.income: Households grouped by where their income falls in the national distribution — a different cut from net worth, since income earned and wealth held are not the same thing.
dimensionNotes.race: Households grouped by the race and ethnicity reported for the reference person, in the categories the Federal Reserve publishes.
dimensionNotes.age: Households grouped by the age of the reference person.

cohort.title: Your cohort
cohort.privacy: Stays in this browser; never sent with a benchmark request.

placements.title: Where your mix lands on every cut
placements.sub: The group your allocation most resembles on each axis. Six readings of the same balance sheet, not six populations: the groups overlap, so these rows do not add up to anything.
placements.notConfident: no close match on this cut
placements.needsApi: This one needs the API: placing a portfolio reads all six axes, and the embedded snapshot carries net worth only.
placements.debtSub: And the same reading for the {amount} you owe. A household can hold assets like one tier and owe like another — a mortgage and a brokerage account are not the same decision.

title.networth: What net worth puts you in each tier
title.income: What income puts you in each band

sub.networth: A threshold, not a shape: this asks how much, where the rest of the page asks how it is held. Net worth means everything you own less everything you owe.
sub.income: A threshold, not a shape: this asks how much a household earns in a year, where the rest of the page asks how its assets are held.

placement.floor: It begins at {amount}, as measured in {quarter}.
placement.belowAll: That is below the {tier}, which begins at {amount}. The Fed publishes no floor below it.
placement.measured: Thresholds come from the Survey of Consumer Finances, which runs every three years; these were last measured in {quarter}, so they are older than the allocations above.

debtBlurbs.home_mortgages: Mortgages secured on owner-occupied property, including home equity lines.
debtBlurbs.consumer_credit: Credit cards, car loans, student loans and other unsecured consumer borrowing.
debtBlurbs.depository_loans: Loans from banks and other depository institutions not classified elsewhere.
debtBlurbs.other_loans: Margin loans, policy loans and other borrowing outside the categories above.
debtBlurbs.deferred_premiums: Life insurance premiums owed but not yet paid — the one liability outside the loan tree.

movers.title: What changed
movers.sub: How {tier} held its assets in {from} against {to}, biggest move first. Shares, not dollars: every tier's balance sheet grew over any long window, so dollars would rank these by asset prices rather than by what changed about the mix.
movers.needsApi: This one needs the API: it compares two quarters, and the embedded snapshot carries the latest one only.

rebalance.title: What it would take to match
rebalance.sub: The arithmetic of the gaps above: {share} of the portfolio would move, in {count} transfers. Descriptive, like the rest of this page — it is what matching would mean, not a suggestion to do it.
rebalance.biggest: Of those, {asset} alone would close the most distance — bringing it to the benchmark raises the similarity by {gain}.

share.copy: Copy a link to this comparison
share.note: The link carries your holdings in it. They stay out of server logs, but anyone you send it to can read them.
share.inUrl: Link put in the address bar — copy it from there.
share.incomingTitle: This link carries a portfolio: {amount} across {count} holdings.
share.incomingReplaces: Showing it replaces the numbers saved in this browser, and there is no undo.
share.incomingEmpty: Nothing is saved in this browser yet.
